interest: This file provides valuable insight into the ideological and legislative mechanisms through which Imperial Japan subordinated religious groups to state control during the 1930s, culminating in the milestone Religious Organizations Law of 1939. It vividly illustrates the dual nature of Japanese religious policy: intense domestic surveillance and doctrinal questionnaires imposed on Christian denominations alongside opportunistic geopolitical courting of the Islamic world as an anti-communist weapon. The papers also capture fascinating diplomatic dimensions, including Italian financing rumors and Turkish diplomatic boycotts surrounding the 1938 Tokyo Mosque dedication, high-level Vatican diplomacy through Cardinal Dougherty's audience with Emperor Hirohito, and the violent spillover of Japanese religious repression into occupied China.
overview: This file comprises the Department of State list of papers (docket sheets) for decimal file 894.404 (Social Matters: Japan - Religion; Church) covering the period from 1933 to 1939. The records catalogued trace Japanese state policy toward various religious denominations—principally Christianity, Islam, and Shinto sects like Tenrikyo—and document increasing governmental surveillance, regulation, and ideological mobilization leading up to the enactment of the comprehensive Religious Organizations Law (Law No. 77) of April 1939. Key topics include Home Ministry inquiries into whether Shrine Shinto constitutes a religion, police questionnaires monitoring Christian bodies, high-profile diplomatic events such as Cardinal Dougherty's audience with the Emperor, Japanese efforts to cultivate Islamic goodwill as an anti-communist bulwark (highlighted by the May 1938 dedication of the Tokyo Mosque attended by foreign Muslim dignitaries), protests regarding Islamic discrimination under the Diet, and reports on the persecution of Christian workers in Japanese-occupied China.

subfiles.about: Transmits a letter introducing Mr. H. Hirayama traveling to the United States to arrange the purchase and distribution of his motion picture depicting the persecution of Japanese Christians.
subfiles.from: Union Christian College of Korea (George S. McCune)
subfiles.summary: George S. McCune of the Union Christian College of Korea introduces Mr. H. Hirayama, who is traveling to the United States to sell or distribute his film 'The Twenty Six Martyrs of Japan.' The film depicts the historic persecution of Christians in Japan during the feudal era. The correspondence was transmitted to the State Department's Division of Far Eastern Affairs.
subfiles.title: Letter from George S. McCune introducing H. Hirayama and 'The Twenty Six Martyrs of Japan' film

subfiles.about: Acknowledges correspondence regarding Hirayama's film and notes handling through diplomatic channels and the Japanese information office.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew acknowledges communications concerning the Japanese cinema project about the early Christian martyrs. He notes liaison with the Japanese information office and coordination through regular diplomatic channels in Washington. The despatch relates to the official handling of cultural and religious publicity abroad.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 62 from Grew regarding diplomatic handling of Japanese cinema mission

subfiles.about: Reports on the Home Ministry Commission's three-year inquiry into whether Shrine Shinto constitutes a religion and its inability to reach a unanimous decision.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet records that a special commission working under the Japanese Home Ministry spent three years investigating whether Shrine Shinto should be classified as a religion. The commission reported that it was unable to reach a unanimous decision and consequently suspended its deliberations for the time being. The full underlying report is filed under 894.00 P.R./62.
subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet on Home Ministry Commission inquiry into State Shinto

subfiles.about: Transmits newspaper clippings from Yokohama reporting on the doctrines and activities of the Tenrikyo religion.
subfiles.summary: Consul Richard F. Boyce in Yokohama transmits clippings from The Japan Advertiser and The Japan Times & Mail dated Sunday, November 4, 1934. The articles provide detailed informational coverage regarding the Tenrikyo religious sect. The original despatch and attached clippings are cross-referenced to file 150.9469/73.
subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet on consular report and press clippings concerning Tenrikyo

subfiles.about: Requests a formal message of greeting from the Department of State or President Roosevelt for the Methodist General Conference in Japan.
subfiles.from: William F. Quillian (Methodist Episcopal Church, South)
subfiles.summary: William F. Quillian of the General Board of Christian Education of the Methodist Episcopal Church, South, writes regarding the upcoming General Conference of the Methodist Church in Japan scheduled for autumn 1935. He asks whether the Department of State or President Franklin D. Roosevelt would be willing to issue a brief statement of greeting and goodwill to the conference. The correspondence was cross-referenced to President Roosevelt's personal file (811.001 Roosevelt, F.D.).
subfiles.title: Letter from William F. Quillian requesting goodwill message for Methodist General Conference in Japan

subfiles.about: Declines to issue or recommend a presidential message of greeting to the Methodist conference in Japan in accordance with diplomatic usage.
subfiles.summary: The Division of Far Eastern Affairs replies to William F. Quillian's inquiry concerning a message to the Methodist conference in Japan. The Department advises that, being contrary to general diplomatic usage and custom, it must regretfully decline to issue a goodwill message or recommend that President Roosevelt do so. The response reflects traditional State Department policy against official endorsements of religious assemblies abroad.
subfiles.title: Letter from Department of State declining goodwill message for Methodist conference

subfiles.about: Quotes foreign press coverage reporting on Muslim activities and the status of Islam in Japan.
subfiles.summary: U.S. Minister to Iran William H. Hornibrook submits Despatch No. 486 quoting a newspaper article regarding the Muslim community in Japan. The document demonstrates international diplomatic observation of Japanese outreach to Islamic nations. The underlying despatch is cross-referenced to decimal file 891.9111/382.
subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet on Despatch No. 486 from Teheran regarding Muslims in Japan

subfiles.about: Reports that a Beirut organization designated an Islamic scholar to travel to Japan at their expense to teach Islam.
subfiles.summary: Consular officer Farrell in Beirut reports that the organization Al-Ahrar al-Masonni (Masonic Free-Thinkers) reportedly selected a learned ulema to travel to Japan at their expense. The mission of this religious scholar was to teach the Mohammedan religion in Japan. The report is cross-referenced to file 890d.9111/106.
subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet on consular report from Beirut regarding Islamic mission to Japan

subfiles.about: Reports on Cardinal Dougherty's reception by Japanese church leaders and his private audiences with Emperor Hirohito and the Apostolic Delegate.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew reports that Cardinal Dennis Dougherty, Archbishop of Philadelphia, was received by various church officials in Japan. Furthermore, Emperor Hirohito received Cardinal Dougherty and the Apostolic Delegate to Japan in separate formal audiences. The original despatch is cross-referenced to file 032-Dougherty, Cardinal 1/1.
subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet on Despatch No. 2276 from Tokyo regarding Cardinal Dougherty's audience with the Emperor

subfiles.about: Transmits a missionary paper analyzing the relations between Christianity, Christian education, and the Japanese state.
subfiles.summary: A. L. Warnshuis of the International Missionary Council transmits a copy of an observational paper written in 1936 by a Christian missionary in Japan. The paper examines the mounting frictions between Christianity and the imperial Japanese state, with specific emphasis on state pressure on Christian educational institutions. The paper is cross-referenced to file 894.1163/6.
subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet on International Missionary Council paper on Christianity and the state in Japan

subfiles.about: Reports on an official Japanese questionnaire circulated to twenty-four Christian organizations inquiring into their doctrines and beliefs.
subfiles.summary: Consul George A. Makinson reports from Osaka that Japanese authorities issued an official questionnaire to twenty-four Christian organizations. The questionnaire demanded written statements clarifying their views and doctrines in relation to state ideology and national polity. The despatch is cross-referenced to file 894.1163/12.
subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet on Despatch from Osaka regarding Japanese official questionnaire to Christian bodies

subfiles.about: Reports on the dedication of Tokyo's first mosque and Japan's strategic cultivation of Islamic leaders as an anti-communist measure.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew reports on the dedication on May 12, 1938, of the first Mohammedan mosque built in Tokyo. He notes that Japanese authorities were actively establishing closer ties with Muslims, viewing Islam as an effective ideological bulwark against Communism. The despatch notes rumors that the Italian government defrayed travel expenses for the Prince of Yemen and Saudi envoy Sheikh Hafiz Wahba, while the Turkish Ambassador declined Foreign Minister Hirota's invitation to attend.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3036 from Grew on dedication of the Tokyo Mosque and Japanese Islamic policy

subfiles.about: Communicates with the Department of State regarding religious matters and missionary work in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Evangelist H. Parker Dunlop addresses a communication to the State Department concerning religious conditions and Christian activities in Japan. The letter relates to ongoing developments affecting Christian evangelism under tightening Japanese governmental supervision. The document was indexed in the Department's Far Eastern registry.
subfiles.title: Letter from H. Parker Dunlop regarding religious matters in Japan

subfiles.about: Reports on proposed Japanese legislation designed to define the legal status of religious organizations and place them under state control.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew forwards Despatch No. 3722 reviewing proposed government legislation aimed at controlling religious organizations in Japan. The bill sought to define the legal status of all religious groups and establish administrative machinery for their comprehensive supervision and regulation. This report provided U.S. diplomats with early analysis of the forthcoming Religious Organizations Law.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3722 from Grew on proposed Religious Organizations Law

subfiles.about: Protests alleged discrimination against the Islamic faith in proceedings of the 74th Japanese Imperial Diet.
subfiles.summary: L. Selim Glick writes to the Division of Far Eastern Affairs concerning the status of Islam in Japan. He encloses a resolution protesting discriminatory measures and attitudes toward the Islamic religion expressed during the 74th session of the Japanese Imperial Diet. The communication reflects grievances among Muslim observers over their statutory exclusion or subordination under the new religious legislation.
subfiles.title: Letter from L. Selim Glick protesting Diet discrimination against Islam

subfiles.about: Transmits an English translation and analysis of the newly promulgated Religious Organizations Law (Law No. 77).
subfiles.summary: Chargé d'Affaires ad interim Eugene H. Dooman reports on the promulgation of the Religious Organizations Law (Law No. 77), which was published in the official Japanese gazette (Kanpō) on April 8, 1939. The despatch encloses an English translation of the enacted law along with legal and political analysis of its regulatory scope over Christian and other religious bodies. The report was noted to the Legal Adviser's Office and cross-referenced to file 894.1163.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3910 from Dooman transmitting the Religious Organizations Law (Law No. 77)

subfiles.about: Summarizes the key regulatory mechanisms and provisions of Japan's newly enacted Religious Organizations Law.
subfiles.summary: The U.S. Military Attaché in Tokyo submits Report No. 9819 detailing the principal provisions of the Religious Organizations Law. The report outlines the statutory authorities assumed by the Japanese government to supervise religious doctrine, approve administrative leadership, and regulate church properties. It highlights the military's assessment of religious regulation as part of Japan's total national mobilization.
subfiles.title: Report No. 9819 from Military Attaché summarizing principal provisions of the Religious Organizations Law

subfiles.about: Reports on instances of persecution and harassment of Christian missionary workers by Japanese authorities in occupied China.
subfiles.summary: Consul Robert Lacy Smyth submits Despatch No. 2151 documenting the persecution of Christian workers in Japanese-occupied China. The document encloses extracts from a letter by missionary Hugh W. Hubbard dated June 28, 1939, and a report from the American Consul at Nanking dated May 16, 1939, detailing concrete cases of harassment and repression. The underlying despatch is cross-referenced to decimal file 893.1163/913.
subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet on Despatch No. 2151 from Smyth on persecution of Christian workers in China
